description_full: Insteel Industries Inc., together with its subsidiaries, manufactures and markets steel wire reinforcing products for concrete construction applications in the United States and internationally. The company offers prestressed concrete strand (PC strand) and welded wire reinforcement (WWR) products. Its PC strand, a seven-wire strand that is used to impart compression forces into precast concrete elements and structures providing reinforcement for bridges, parking decks, buildings, and other concrete structures. The company's WWR engineered reinforcing product is used in non-residential and residential construction. It also produces a range of WWR products, such as engineered structural mesh, an engineered made-to-order product that is used as the primary reinforcement for concrete elements or structures serving as a reinforcing solution for hot-rolled rebar; concrete pipe reinforcement, an engineered made-to-order product, which is used as the primary reinforcement in concrete pipe, box culverts, and precast manholes for drainage and sewage systems, water treatment facilities, and other related applications; and standard welded wire reinforcement, a secondary reinforcing product for crack control applications in residential and light non-residential construction, including driveways, sidewalks, and various slab-on-grade applications. The company serves manufacturers of concrete products, distributors, rebar fabricators, and contractors through a network of sales representatives. Insteel Industries Inc. was founded in 1953 and is headquartered in Mount Airy, North Carolina.

financial_summary: Insteel Industries, Inc. is a small-cap industrials business with a $518M market cap on $740M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +4% over the past three years and +6% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.

Returns on capital run at 11% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business barely earns its keep economically, and 12% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $25M in free cash flow — roughly 3 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.24× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year.

Shareholder yield of 4.8% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 5.1% of the shares, and profit capture is only 0.5× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sect: Its 5% operating margin is roughly in line with the Industrials median (9%).
It captures well under its share of sector profits (0.47x its revenue share).
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-21.0% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 544 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are roughly flat over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 30% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 40% and a beta of 0.89, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y -0.26 vs 5y 0.84), so read it loosely.
About $4.1M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 58% in the 2020 crash, 47% in the 2022 bear market and 75% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $21.69 (margin of safety -23%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 42%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $16.62 to $29.19 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Industrials peers: P/E 17.7 vs 23.3 and EV/EBITDA 8.7 vs 13.3 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 20% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 4.8% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 7.9% (vs the 8% bar).
The Street target $37.00 on average, 38% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 11% earns above the cost of capital of 9.2%, but the 2pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.85).
It runs a 12% gross margin and converts 3% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.24x.
ROE of 8% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.3x equity multiplier).
It spends 0.5% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $35.0M.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 6.2, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 4.4% over 3 years, 4.6% over 5 years and 5.9% over 10 years, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 16%).
At current returns, reinvesting 25% of profits supports about 2.7% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
Free cash flow has compounded -13.9% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex runs only 0.7x depreciation (1.6% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 7, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own 5.1%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 85%.
It returns 4.8% a year to shareholders (0.6% in buybacks and 0.4% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 21 consecutive years, though it has been cut 7.0% a year over the last five.
people: With about 983 employees, each generates about $752K of revenue, 2.0x the Industrials median, and productivity has risen 5.4% a year.
That works out to $25K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.3M (3x revenue per employee).
